poster.text: Before you value a company you must know what type of company it is, because the category determines how you should read the numbers. Lynch distinguishes six types. Slow growers are mature giants that grow marginally and mainly reward owners with a dividend. Stalwarts are large, stable companies growing at roughly ten to twelve percent — they protect the portfolio in downturns. Fast growers are smaller, aggressive companies growing twenty to twenty-five percent a year — this is where the big winners are found, but also the risk that growth suddenly brakes. Cyclicals such as steel, car and airline companies swing with the business cycle: profitability arrives in waves. Turnarounds are companies in crisis that can turn around — with no correlation to the stock exchange, but with the risk of losing everything looming large. Asset plays are companies with hidden assets — land, patents, cash, tax advantages — that the market has not priced in. The category determines what you should look at, how the valuation is done and when it is time to sell.

Fast growers have the greatest potential but fall hard when growth unexpectedly fades — deceleration is the most dangerous event in this category. Cyclicals fool investors because they look cheapest at the top of the cycle, when P/E is at its lowest, and most expensive at the bottom — the opposite of intuition. Turnarounds can go to zero — here the balance sheet makes the difference between a temporary crisis and bankruptcy. Asset plays demand patience: nobody knows when the market will discover the value, and liabilities can eat the assets during the wait. Match the category to your risk tolerance, your time and your ability to monitor.

poster.text: The P/E ratio — the price divided by earnings per share — states how many years of current earnings you are paying for the stock. A P/E of 12 means you are paying twelve years of current earnings; a P/E of 40 means forty years. Lynch stresses that P/E should be compared against three reference points: the company's own history, the industry average and — most important — the growth rate. A P/E of 15 is cheap at thirty percent growth and expensive at zero percent growth. A high P/E means high expectations, and expectations are punished hard when they fail: a stock at P/E 40 that misses its budget can be halved. A low P/E, on the other hand, can be a value trap, especially in cyclical companies where earnings stand at their peak. Lynch also argues that the average P/E of the entire stock exchange says something about the market's total optimism. The rule: never read P/E in isolation — it is a story measure, not a fact sheet.

poster.text: Perhaps the most important truth in the book: the share price follows earnings per share over time. In the short run, of course, mood and sentiment can drive a stock any which way; in the long run it is earnings growth that dominates. When earnings grow twenty percent a year the price tends to follow — the P/E multiple simply swings around that line. poster.text: Profit can either be reinvested, paid out as a dividend or used for share buybacks of the company's own stocks. poster.text: The PEG ratio ties valuation and growth together: P/E divided by the expected growth rate. A rule of thumb is that a PEG around one is reasonably valued, below one potentially cheap and well above one expensive. The number makes it possible to compare companies with different growth rates: a company with P/E thirty and thirty percent growth (PEG one) can be cheaper than one with P/E fifteen and five percent growth (PEG three). But the limitations are at least as important as the number. Growth forecasts are guesses — PEG is only as good as the assumption. The number does not account for risk, not for dividends and not for how long the growth can continue. Cyclical companies give misleading PEG figures, because earnings stand at their peak when P/E is at its lowest. Lynch used the relationship between P/E and growth as a starting point — never as a decision rule. Also compare with the company's own historical range: a fast grower that has always traded at PEG one and a half and that suddenly stands at zero point eight deserves investigation. But no multiple replaces understanding of the business.

poster.text: Financial statement analysis becomes manageable if you follow a fixed workflow. Step one: read the income statement — revenue, margins and earnings per share. What is the trend? The point is not to predict the future perfectly — it is to build a repeatable process that makes you better every quarter.
